notes.front: What is statement testing?
notes.back: A white-box test technique whose coverage items are the executable statements in the code.
notes.explanation: Tests are designed to run statements until an acceptable level of coverage is reached.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a proofreader ticking off each line of a contract as it is read aloud, until enough lines have been ticked.

notes.front: What is statement coverage?
notes.back: “The coverage of executable source statements.”
notes.explanation: It is the figure that statement testing works to raise.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “statement coverage”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The coverage of executable source statements.
notes.example: Like running a highlighter over each line of code as the tests execute it; the highlighted share is the statement coverage.

notes.front: What is a control flow graph?
notes.back: A graph showing the possible sequences in which a test object's source code statements are executed.
notes.explanation: It turns code into points and connections, which white-box techniques can then count.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a railway map of the code: stations are points in the program, and tracks show where execution can go next.

notes.front: In white-box testing, what is a branch?
notes.back: A transfer of control between two nodes in the control flow graph.
notes.explanation: Every move from one point of the code to the next is a branch, whether or not a decision is involved.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like one stretch of track between two stations on a railway map.

notes.front: What is branch testing?
notes.back: A white-box test technique whose coverage items are branches.
notes.explanation: Tests are designed to exercise branches until an acceptable level of coverage is reached.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like following every arrow on a flowchart: the plain arrows between steps as well as the yes and no arrows leaving each question.

notes.front: What is branch coverage?
notes.back: “The coverage of branches in a control flow graph.”
notes.explanation: It is the figure that branch testing works to raise.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “branch coverage”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The coverage of branches in a control flow graph.
notes.example: Like the share of a flowchart's arrows that the tests have followed.

notes.front: What is error guessing?
notes.back: “A test technique in which the tests conditions are based on the tester's knowledge of past failures or failure modes.”
notes.explanation: The tester uses what has gone wrong before to predict what may go wrong now.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “error guessing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test technique in which the tests conditions are based on the tester's knowledge of past failures or failure modes.
notes.example: Like a locksmith who first tries the tricks that opened similar locks before.

notes.front: What is a fault attack?
notes.back: A way to implement error guessing: the tester builds a list of possible errors, defects and failures, and designs tests aimed at them.
notes.explanation: It makes error guessing systematic by working from a written list.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a security tester working down a list of known ways into a building: an open window, a propped fire door, a borrowed pass.

notes.front: What is exploratory testing?
notes.back: “A test approach in which tests are dynamically designed and executed based on tester's knowledge, exploration of a test item, and previous test results.”
notes.explanation: Each next test is chosen from what the last ones revealed, not fixed in advance.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “exploratory testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test approach in which tests are dynamically designed and executed based on tester's knowledge, exploration of a test item, and previous test results.
notes.example: Like exploring a new city without a fixed route, choosing each next street from what you have just seen.

notes.front: In exploratory testing, what is a test charter?
notes.back: A brief containing test objectives that guides the tester through an exploratory test session.
notes.explanation: It gives a session its direction without scripting the steps.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a brief for a scouting trip: “explore the refund flow for part-paid orders and look for rounding problems”.

notes.front: What is session-based testing?
notes.back: A way to structure exploratory testing: it is performed within a defined time box, guided by a test charter.
notes.explanation: The time box and the charter give freely designed tests a clear frame.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a timed exam slot: the work happens inside a fixed block of time, against a set brief.

notes.front: What is checklist-based testing?
notes.back: “An experience-based test technique in which test cases are designed to exercise the items of a checklist.”
notes.explanation: The checklist, built from experience, decides what the tests must touch.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “checklist-based testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: An experience-based test technique in which test cases are designed to exercise the items of a checklist.
notes.example: Like a pilot's pre-flight checklist, where each item is checked in turn.

notes.front: What is a collaboration-based test approach?
notes.back: “An approach to testing that focuses on defect avoidance by collaborating among stakeholders.”
notes.explanation: The aim is to stop defects arising, not only to find them afterwards.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “collaboration-based test approach”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: An approach to testing that focuses on defect avoidance by collaborating among stakeholders.
notes.example: Like a client, an architect and a builder walking through the plans together so mistakes are caught before any bricks are laid.

notes.front: What is a user story?
notes.back: A description of a feature that will be valuable to either a user or a purchaser of a system or software.
notes.explanation: It frames work around the value someone gets, not around a technical task.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a sticky note on a team board describing one feature a shopper would value, such as saving a basket for later.

notes.front: What does INVEST stand for in user stories?
notes.back: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable: the qualities of a good user story.
notes.explanation: Each letter names one quality a team can check a story against.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a pre-flight check for stories: before a story goes into work, the team runs it past six questions.

notes.front: What are acceptance criteria?
notes.back: “The criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders.”
notes.explanation: They turn “done” into conditions everyone can check.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “acceptance criteria”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The criteria that a work product must satisfy to be accepted by the stakeholders.
notes.example: Like the conditions a buyer sets before paying for a house survey: the report must cover the roof, the damp and the drains.

notes.front: What is acceptance test-driven development (ATDD)?
notes.back: “A collaboration-based test-first approach that defines acceptance tests in the stakeholders' domain language.”
notes.explanation: The tests are agreed before the build, in words the stakeholders themselves use.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “acceptance test-driven development”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A collaboration-based test-first approach that defines acceptance tests in the stakeholders' domain language.
notes.example: Like agreeing the driving test's marking sheet before the lessons start, written in words both learner and examiner use.

notes.front: In ATDD, what is a specification workshop?
notes.back: The first step, where team members analyse, discuss and write the user story and, if not yet defined, its acceptance criteria.
notes.explanation: It settles what the story means before any test case is written.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a planning meeting where a product owner, a developer and a tester talk one story through until they agree what it means.

notes.front: Which two code-related white-box test techniques does the v4.0.1 syllabus focus on?
notes.back: Statement testing and branch testing.
notes.explanation: More rigorous white-box techniques exist but are left out of the Foundation syllabus.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3 White-Box Test Techniques, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which white-box technique did branch testing replace in the v4.0 Foundation syllabus?
notes.back: Decision testing, together with decision coverage.
notes.explanation: Reasons given include branch coverage being more common in practice and standards defining “decision” differently.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 10 Appendix C – Release Notes, p. 75
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the aim of statement testing?
notes.back: To design tests that run the code's statements until the team reaches a level of coverage it accepts.
notes.explanation: The target is a level of coverage the team accepts, not necessarily every statement.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is statement coverage measured?
notes.back: Statements exercised by the test cases, divided by the total number of executable statements in the code, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: Only executable statements count, so comments and blank lines do not affect it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does 100% statement coverage ensure?
notes.back: That all executable statements in the code have been exercised at least once.
notes.explanation: No line of the code has been left unrun by the tests.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Once 100% statement coverage is reached, every faulty statement has run at least once, and that {{c1::may}} lead to a visible failure.
notes.back: May.
notes.explanation: Running a faulty statement is necessary for the failure to show, but it is not enough on its own.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does 100% statement coverage ensure that all the decision logic has been tested?
notes.back: No; it may not exercise all the branches in the code.
notes.explanation: Every line can run while some decision outcomes are never taken.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an unconditional branch?
notes.back: A transfer of control in straight-line code.
notes.explanation: Execution simply moves on to the next point; no decision is made.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a conditional branch?
notes.back: A transfer of control that is a decision outcome.
notes.explanation: Which way execution goes depends on how the decision turns out.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where do conditional branches typically come from?
notes.back: True or false outcomes of “if...then” decisions, outcomes of switch/case statements, and decisions to exit or continue a loop.
notes.explanation: Each outcome is its own branch, so branch testing must take every one of them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the aim of branch testing?
notes.back: To design tests that take the code's branches until the team reaches a level of coverage it accepts.
notes.explanation: As with statement testing, the target is an acceptable level, which the team decides.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is branch coverage measured?
notes.back: Branches exercised by the test cases, divided by the total number of branches, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: Unconditional and conditional branches both count.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does “branch coverage subsumes statement coverage” mean?
notes.back: Any set of test cases achieving 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage.
notes.explanation: Taking every branch necessarily runs every statement along the way.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does 100% statement coverage guarantee 100% branch coverage?
notes.back: No; subsumption works only from branch coverage to statement coverage.
notes.explanation: An “if” with no “else” shows it: one test can run every line while the false outcome is never taken.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of defect may 100% branch coverage still miss?
notes.back: A defect that needs a specific path through the code to be executed.
notes.explanation: Taking every branch at some point does not mean taking every combination of branches in one run.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What fundamental strength do all white-box test techniques share?
notes.back: They take the whole of the implementation into account.
notes.explanation: That helps defect detection even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of defect may white-box testing fail to detect?
notes.back: Defects of omission, where the software does not implement one or more requirements.
notes.explanation: The tests look at what was implemented, so a requirement that was never implemented may go unnoticed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are white-box techniques well suited to reviewing?
notes.back: Code not yet ready for execution, pseudocode, and other high-level logic that can be modelled with a control flow graph.
notes.explanation: None of these needs to run for its structure to be analysed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does performing only black-box testing fail to provide?
notes.back: A measure of actual code coverage.
notes.explanation: Black-box tests are designed from the specification, so they say nothing about how much code they reach.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do white-box coverage measures provide?
notes.back: An objective coverage figure, plus the information needed to design extra tests that raise it.
notes.explanation: Raising coverage this way in turn increases confidence in the code.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three experience-based test techniques does the v4.0.1 syllabus discuss?
notes.back: Error guessing, exploratory testing and checklist-based testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls these the commonly used ones.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4 Experience-based Test Techniques, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In error guessing, which kind of knowledge concerns how the application itself has behaved?
notes.back: How the application has worked in the past.
notes.explanation: Its own history shows where it is likely to fail again.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In error guessing, which kind of knowledge concerns the people who write the code?
notes.back: The types of errors developers tend to make, and the types of defects those errors cause.
notes.explanation: Habitual human mistakes leave predictable kinds of defect behind.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In error guessing, which kind of knowledge comes from outside the application under test?
notes.back: The types of failures that have occurred in other, similar applications.
notes.explanation: Failures seen elsewhere suggest where a similar product may fail too.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a fault attack, what must the tester first create or acquire?
notes.back: A list of possible errors, defects and failures.
notes.explanation: The tests are then designed item by item from that list.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can fault attack lists be built from?
notes.back: Experience, defect and failure data, or common knowledge about why software fails.
notes.explanation: The list can come from the tester's own work or from what is widely known.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What three things is exploratory testing used for?
notes.back: Learning more about the test object, exploring it more deeply with focused tests, and creating tests for untested areas.
notes.explanation: Each use grows out of the tester learning about the test object while testing it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What usually follows an exploratory test session?
notes.back: A debriefing: a discussion between the tester and stakeholders interested in the session's test results.
notes.explanation: It passes what the session found to the people who need it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In session-based testing, how may the test objectives be treated?
notes.back: As high-level test conditions.
notes.explanation: The charter's objectives then play the part that test conditions play in scripted testing.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In session-based testing, when are coverage items identified?
notes.back: During the test session, where they are also exercised.
notes.explanation: They emerge as the tester explores rather than being listed beforehand.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What state of the specifications makes exploratory testing useful?
notes.back: Few or inadequate specifications.
notes.explanation: With little written down, the tester learns about the test object while testing it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides poor specifications, what project pressure makes exploratory testing useful?
notes.back: Significant time pressure on the testing.
notes.explanation: It is one of two such situations the syllabus names, alongside thin specifications.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can exploratory testing relate to more formal test techniques?
notes.back: It is useful to complement them.
notes.explanation: It adds tests for areas the formal techniques did not reach.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can exploratory testing incorporate other test techniques?
notes.back: Yes, for example equivalence partitioning.
notes.explanation: Exploring freely does not stop a tester using a systematic technique mid-session.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In checklist-based testing, what does the tester do?
notes.back: Designs, implements and executes tests to cover test conditions from a checklist.
notes.explanation: The checklist supplies the test conditions; the tester still builds and runs the tests.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can checklists be built from?
notes.back: Experience, knowledge of what is important for the user, or an understanding of why and how software fails.
notes.explanation: This is what makes checklist-based testing an experience-based technique.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should a checklist include items that can be checked automatically?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: It is one of three kinds of item the syllabus says to keep off checklists, alongside over-general items and ones better suited as entry or exit criteria.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should a checklist include items that would work better as conditions for starting or finishing testing?
notes.back: No; such items are better suited as entry or exit criteria.
notes.explanation: Those decide whether an activity may start or end, not what a test should examine.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should a checklist include items that are very general?
notes.back: No; items that are too general should be left out.
notes.explanation: A vague item cannot be checked separately and directly.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What should be possible for each checklist item?
notes.back: Checking it separately and directly.
notes.explanation: Each item should stand alone, without depending on another item's result.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why may some checklist entries become less effective over time?
notes.back: Developers learn to avoid making the same errors.
notes.explanation: This, together with newly found severe defects, is why checklists need regular updates.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Checklists should be regularly updated based on {{c1::defect analysis}}.
notes.back: Defect analysis.
notes.explanation: Analysing defects shows which entries still find problems and which are missing.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What should be avoided when adding entries to a checklist?
notes.back: Letting the checklist become too long.
notes.explanation: Updating a checklist means pruning as well as adding.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Without detailed test cases, what can checklist-based testing provide?
notes.back: Guidelines and some degree of consistency for the testing.
notes.explanation: Testers without scripts still share a common list to work from.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the likely effect of high-level checklists?
notes.back: Testers vary more in what they actually do: coverage may grow, but runs are harder to repeat.
notes.explanation: Testers fill in the details differently, so runs differ from one another.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides defect detection, what do collaboration-based approaches also focus on?
notes.back: Defect avoidance, through collaboration and communication.
notes.explanation: Talking early is meant to stop defects being written in the first place.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5 Collaboration-based Test Approaches, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 3 C's of a user story, what is the Card?
notes.back: The medium that describes the user story, physical or electronic.
notes.explanation: It is where the story is written down, not the whole of the story.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 3 C's of a user story, what does the Conversation explain?
notes.back: How the software will be used. It can be documented or verbal.
notes.explanation: Much of a story's detail lives in the team's discussion rather than on the card.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 3 C's of a user story, what is the Confirmation?
notes.back: The acceptance criteria.
notes.explanation: They confirm when the story has been delivered as intended.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The most common user story format is: As a [role], I want [goal to be accomplished], {{c1::so that I can [resulting business value for the role]}}.
notes.back: so that I can [resulting business value for the role]
notes.explanation: The last part ties the story to the value it brings to the role.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three perspectives does collaborative user story writing take into account?
notes.back: Business, development and testing.
notes.explanation: Together they give the team a shared vision of what should be delivered.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the I stand for?
notes.back: Independent.
notes.explanation: A good story does not rely on another story to be delivered or tested.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the N stand for?
notes.back: Negotiable.
notes.explanation: The details of a good story stay open to discussion.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the V stand for?
notes.back: Valuable.
notes.explanation: A good story delivers something that matters to a user or purchaser.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the first E stand for?
notes.back: Estimable.
notes.explanation: The team must be able to judge how much work a good story needs.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the S stand for?
notes.back: Small.
notes.explanation: A good story is a modest piece of work, not a whole project.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In INVEST, what does the T stand for?
notes.back: Testable.
notes.explanation: Someone must be able to tell whether a good story has been delivered.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If a stakeholder does not know how to test a user story, what may that indicate?
notes.back: That the story is unclear or not valuable to them, or simply that they need help with testing.
notes.explanation: Not knowing how to test a story is a warning sign worth following up.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From a testing point of view, how may acceptance criteria be viewed?
notes.back: As the test conditions that the tests should exercise.
notes.explanation: They state what an implementation must meet, which is what tests check.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of the 3 C's do acceptance criteria usually result from?
notes.back: The Conversation.
notes.explanation: Discussing how the software will be used brings out the conditions it must meet.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of acceptance criteria settles what a user story does and does not include?
notes.back: Defining the scope of the user story.
notes.explanation: Clear criteria mark the story's edges.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of acceptance criteria concerns agreement among the people involved?
notes.back: Reaching consensus among the stakeholders.
notes.explanation: Written criteria give stakeholders one shared statement to agree on.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of acceptance criteria covers both what should happen and how errors are handled?
notes.back: Describing both positive and negative scenarios.
notes.explanation: The criteria cover the unhappy cases as well as the expected ones.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of acceptance criteria links them to testing the finished story?
notes.back: Serving as a basis for the user story acceptance testing.
notes.explanation: The acceptance tests are built from the criteria.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which use of acceptance criteria helps the team forecast its work?
notes.back: Allowing accurate planning and estimation.
notes.explanation: Knowing exactly what must be met makes the effort easier to judge.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the two most common formats for writing acceptance criteria?
notes.back: Scenario-oriented and rule-oriented.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says most acceptance criteria can be written in one of the two.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: May a team write acceptance criteria in its own custom format?
notes.back: Yes, as long as the criteria are well-defined and unambiguous.
notes.explanation: The format matters less than whether the criteria are clear.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, when are the test cases created?
notes.back: Before the user story is implemented.
notes.explanation: ATDD is a test-first approach, so the tests lead the development.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, who creates the test cases?
notes.back: Team members with different perspectives, for example customers, developers and testers.
notes.explanation: Mixing perspectives is what makes the approach collaboration-based.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Must ATDD test cases be automated?
notes.back: No; they may be executed manually or automated.
notes.explanation: The approach is about writing tests first, not about how they are run.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus's summary of test-first approaches, what does ATDD derive tests from?
notes.back: Acceptance criteria, as part of the system design process.
notes.explanation: The tests are written before the part of the application they check is developed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 Testing as a Driver for Software Development, p. 26
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is resolved during an ATDD specification workshop?
notes.back: Incompleteness, ambiguities or defects in the user story.
notes.explanation: Problems in the story are dealt with before any code or tests are written.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the ATDD step after the specification workshop, and who does it?
notes.back: Creating the test cases, done by the team as a whole or by the tester individually.
notes.explanation: Either way, the tests rest on what the workshop agreed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, what are the test cases based on?
notes.back: The acceptance criteria. They can be seen as examples of how the software works.
notes.explanation: Examples of expected behaviour help the team implement the story correctly.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, which test cases typically come first?
notes.back: Positive tests: the expected, error-free path through the story's activities.
notes.explanation: They follow the sequence of activities when everything goes as expected.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, what should the team do once the positive test cases are done?
notes.back: Perform negative testing.
notes.explanation: Once the expected path is pinned down, the team turns to what should happen when things go wrong.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ATDD, what does the team cover last?
notes.back: Non-functional quality characteristics, such as performance efficiency or usability.
notes.explanation: Functional behaviour, positive then negative, comes before these.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How are ATDD test cases typically expressed?
notes.back: In natural-language sentences stakeholders understand, stating any preconditions, the inputs and the postconditions.
notes.explanation: Tests in the stakeholders' language let them check what is being agreed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How much of the user story must ATDD test cases cover?
notes.back: All the characteristics of the user story.
notes.explanation: Any characteristic left without a test is left unconfirmed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do ATDD acceptance tests become executable requirements?
notes.back: Once written in a format an automation framework supports, developers automate them with supporting code while building the story.
notes.explanation: The agreed tests then run as checks of the requirements themselves.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are three of the areas that errors, defects and failures may generally be related to?
notes.back: Any three of: input, output, logic, computation, interfaces and data.
notes.explanation: Grouping past problems by area gives error guessing a structured place to start.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Code: total = price; if member: total = total × 0.9; print(total). One test runs it with member = true. What statement coverage does it give?
notes.back: 100%: every executable statement runs.
notes.explanation: With member true, the discount line runs too, so no statement is left out.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Code: total = price; if member: total = total × 0.9; print(total). One test runs it with member = true. Does it give 100% branch coverage?
notes.back: No: the false outcome of “if member” is never taken.
notes.choices:
A) No, the false outcome is never taken
B) Yes, every statement ran
C) Yes, the code has only one decision
notes.choicesExplained: B: running every statement is statement coverage, which does not ensure every branch. C: one decision still has two outcomes to exercise.
notes.explanation: Full statement coverage does not guarantee full branch coverage.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A control flow graph has 20 branches. Tests exercise 15. What is the branch coverage?
notes.explanation: Branch coverage is branches exercised over all branches: 15 ÷ 20.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A statement copies a customer's name into a 30-character field. Tests run it only with short names and reach 100% statement coverage. What may they have missed?
notes.back: A data-dependent defect, such as a failure with names over 30 characters.
notes.choices:
A) A data-dependent defect with long names
B) Nothing: 100% statement coverage finds every defect
C) Only defects in statements that never ran
notes.choicesExplained: B: exercising a statement will not detect defects in all cases. C: at 100% statement coverage every statement ran.
notes.explanation: Running the statement is not enough if the values that make it fail are never used.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 Statement Testing and Statement Coverage, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Code has two decisions in a row. Tests take true–true and false–false, reaching 100% branch coverage. A defect shows only on the true–false path. Why was it missed?
notes.back: Branch coverage may miss defects that need a specific path to be executed.
notes.explanation: Both outcomes of each decision were taken, but never in that combination.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The requirements say a refund must trigger a confirmation email. The code never sends one. The team has 100% branch coverage. Why did white-box testing not catch this?
notes.back: It is a defect of omission: missing code has no branches for white-box tests to cover.
notes.choices:
A) It is a defect of omission
B) Branch coverage was really lower than 100%
C) Emails cannot be tested
notes.choicesExplained: B: coverage can be complete for the code that exists. C: nothing stops a black-box test checking for the email.
notes.explanation: White-box testing may not detect defects where requirements were never implemented.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A legacy billing system's specification is ten years out of date. Which category of technique still takes the whole implementation into account?
notes.back: White-box test techniques.
notes.choices:
A) White-box test techniques
B) Black-box test techniques
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: B: black-box techniques rest on the specification, which is out of date. C: white-box techniques work from the code itself.
notes.explanation: Their strength is considering the entire implementation, even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A manager asks what percentage of the code a purely black-box regression suite has exercised. Can the suite's results answer that?
notes.back: No; black-box testing alone gives no measure of actual code coverage.
notes.choices:
A) No, a white-box measure is needed
B) Yes, from the number of test cases
C) Yes, from the number of requirements covered
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: counting tests or requirements says nothing about how much code ran.
notes.explanation: A white-box coverage measure would be needed for that figure.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 The Value of White-box Testing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Last year's release crashed on 29 February, so a tester adds leap-day dates to this year's tests. Which technique is this?
notes.back: Error guessing.
notes.choices:
A) Error guessing
B) Exploratory testing
C) Checklist-based testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tests were planned from a past failure, not designed while learning. C: no checklist is being worked through.
notes.explanation: The tests come from knowledge of how the application has failed in the past.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester takes a published list of common web application failures and designs a test to provoke each one. What is this?
notes.back: A fault attack.
notes.choices:
A) A fault attack
B) Checklist-based testing
C) Session-based testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: checklist items are test conditions to cover, not failures to provoke. C: there is no time-boxed session guided by a charter.
notes.explanation: It works from a list of possible failures to design tests that cause them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A sign-up form refuses a perfectly correct email address. In error guessing's list of areas, where does this belong?
notes.back: Input.
notes.explanation: Correct input not being accepted is an input problem.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: One component sends a price in pence; the component receiving it expects pounds. In error guessing's list of areas, where does this belong?
notes.back: Interfaces.
notes.explanation: A mismatch in what two parts pass each other is an interface problem.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 Error Guessing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new mobile app has almost no written specification and must ship in two days. Which experience-based technique does the syllabus say is useful here?
notes.back: Exploratory testing.
notes.choices:
A) Exploratory testing
B) Checklist-based testing
C) Fault attack
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both can help, but the syllabus names exploratory testing for thin specifications and time pressure.
notes.explanation: It is useful when specifications are few or inadequate and time pressure is significant.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester spends a 60-minute block exploring currency conversion, guided by a brief with objectives, then meets the product owner to discuss what was found. What are the brief and the meeting?
notes.back: The test charter and the debriefing of session-based testing.
notes.explanation: A charter guides a time-boxed session, which is usually followed by a debriefing with stakeholders.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 Exploratory Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester works through a list of questions such as “Does every page offer a way back to the home page?”. Which technique is this?
notes.back: Checklist-based testing.
notes.choices:
A) Checklist-based testing
B) Error guessing
C) Exploratory testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: the tests come from a list of conditions, not from anticipated failures. C: the tests are not being designed while exploring.
notes.explanation: The tests cover test conditions taken from a checklist of questions.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A draft checklist includes “Is the code free of compile errors?” and “Is the software good?”. What is wrong with these items?
notes.back: The first can be checked automatically and the second is too general.
notes.explanation: Checklists should leave out automatic checks and over-general items.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 44
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two testers run the same high-level checklist and test quite different things. What trade-off does this show?
notes.back: Potentially greater coverage, but less repeatability.
notes.explanation: High-level checklists leave room for variability in the actual testing.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A checklist item about unclosed database connections has found nothing for a year, while a new high-severity defect type keeps appearing. What should the team do?
notes.back: Update the checklist from defect analysis, adding the new defect type, while keeping the list from growing too long.
notes.explanation: Entries lose effectiveness as developers learn, and new serious defects call for new entries.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 Checklist-Based Testing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before coding starts, a tester, a developer and a business analyst talk through a story to prevent misunderstandings. What is the main focus of this kind of approach?
notes.back: Defect avoidance, through collaboration and communication.
notes.choices:
A) Defect avoidance
B) Measuring code coverage
C) Automating regression tests
notes.choicesExplained: B: no code exists yet to measure. C: the talk is about shared understanding, not about automating tests.
notes.explanation: Collaboration-based approaches focus on avoiding defects, not only detecting them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5 Collaboration-based Test Approaches, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team meets to discuss how a shopper will use a new wishlist feature. Which of the 3 C's is this?
notes.back: Conversation.
notes.choices:
A) Card
B) Conversation
C) Confirmation
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Card is the medium the story is written on. C: the Confirmation is the acceptance criteria.
notes.explanation: The Conversation explains how the software will be used, and it can be verbal.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of these follows the common user story format?
notes.back: As a commuter, I want to save my usual route, so that I can check delays in one tap.
notes.choices:
A) As a commuter, I want to save my usual route, so that I can check delays in one tap.
B) The system shall store routes in the database.
C) Fix the route-saving bug by Friday.
notes.choicesExplained: B: it states a system requirement with no role or value. C: it is a task, with no role, goal or value.
notes.explanation: It names a role, a goal and the value the role gets.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A story cannot be started until two other stories are finished. Which INVEST quality does it most clearly lack?
notes.back: Independent.
notes.choices:
A) Independent
B) Valuable
C) Negotiable
notes.choicesExplained: B: the story may still deliver value once done. C: nothing suggests its details are closed to discussion.
notes.explanation: Its reliance on other stories is exactly what the I in INVEST warns against.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 Collaborative User Story Writing, p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An acceptance criterion reads: “Given a basket with three items, when the shopper removes one, then the total drops by that item's price.” Which format is it?
notes.back: Scenario-oriented.
notes.choices:
A) Scenario-oriented
B) Rule-oriented
C) Not a valid acceptance criterion
notes.choicesExplained: B: rule-oriented criteria are verification lists or input–output tables. C: the criterion is well-defined and unambiguous.
notes.explanation: The criterion is written as a scenario in three parts: a starting situation, an action and the expected result.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During planning, a developer says a story is hard to size because nobody knows what “done” means. Which use of acceptance criteria would help?
notes.back: Allowing accurate planning and estimation.
notes.explanation: Criteria state exactly what must be met, which is what an estimate needs.

notes.front: In a specification workshop for a voucher story, the team notices nobody has said what happens to expired vouchers. What should happen?
notes.back: The team resolves the gap in the workshop, adding to the story or its acceptance criteria.
notes.choices:
A) Resolve it in the workshop
B) Leave it for the developers to decide in code
C) Raise it as a failure after release
notes.choicesExplained: B: ATDD settles such questions before implementation. C: the point of the workshop is to catch it before it becomes a defect.
notes.explanation: Incompleteness and ambiguities in the story are resolved during the specification workshop.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For a “reset password” story, an ATDD team has three test ideas: a valid reset link works; an expired link is refused; the reset page loads within two seconds. In what order should they be covered?
notes.back: Valid link first, then expired link, then page load time.
notes.explanation: ATDD typically goes positive, then negative, then non-functional.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: While writing ATDD tests for a “save basket” story, a tester adds a test for sharing baskets by email, which no story mentions. What is wrong?
notes.back: ATDD test cases should not go beyond the user story.
notes.choices:
A) It goes beyond the story
B) It is a negative test written too early
C) Nothing: extra tests are always welcome
notes.choicesExplained: B: the problem is scope, not order. C: the syllabus says ATDD tests should not go beyond the story.
notes.explanation: The tests must cover the whole story and nothing outside it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two ATDD test cases for a login story both check that a correct password lets the user in. What rule does this break?
notes.back: No two test cases should describe the same characteristics of the user story.
notes.explanation: Each characteristic needs its own single test.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 Acceptance Test-driven Development (ATDD), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the coverage items of statement testing and branch testing differ?
notes.back: Statement testing counts executable statements; branch testing counts branches, the transfers of control in the control flow graph.
notes.explanation: Any test set reaching 100% branch coverage also reaches 100% statement coverage, but not the reverse.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 Branch Testing and Branch Coverage, p. 43
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do scenario-oriented acceptance criteria differ from rule-oriented ones?
notes.back: Scenario-oriented criteria describe scenarios, such as Given/When/Then; rule-oriented criteria use verification lists or input–output tables.
notes.explanation: Most acceptance criteria can be written in one of the two formats.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 Acceptance Criteria, p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus's summary of test-first approaches, how does ATDD differ from TDD?
notes.back: ATDD derives tests from acceptance criteria; TDD directs the coding through test cases.
notes.explanation: Both write tests before the code, but ATDD starts from what stakeholders will accept.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 Testing as a Driver for Software Development, p. 26
